The New York Times, editorial feature

venues.name: Le Sherpa
venues.note: A long-running farm-to-table favourite with a leafy garden and a Saturday market that draws the whole city.
credentials: TripAdvisor Travellers' Choice

venues.name: Pashupatinath Temple & the Bagmati aarti
venues.note: One of the most sacred Shiva shrines in the Hindu world, its gilded pagoda roof rising over the Bagmati where the smoke of the cremation ghats never quite settles. For an Indian family the pull is instant and deep, the same Shiva of Kashi, the same river-and-fire theology, and at dusk the Bagmati Aarti of lamps and conch on the far bank is one of the most moving rituals in South Asia. Only Hindus enter the inner sanctum; a knowledgeable guide reads the ghats and the sadhus without intruding.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: Boudhanath Stupa & the evening kora
venues.note: One of the largest stupas on earth, a vast white dome crowned by the all-seeing Buddha eyes, ringed by red-robed monks, butter lamps and the murmur of Om Mani Padme Hum. At dusk the whole Tibetan quarter walks the kora clockwise around it, prayer wheels spinning, a slow, hypnotic circuit that multi-generational families can join at their own pace. Take a rooftop café table on the circle for the finest seat in Kathmandu.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: The Tibetan quarter around Boudha
venues.note: The lanes radiating off the stupa are the heart of the Tibetan diaspora in Nepal, monasteries (gompas) of every lineage, thangka ateliers, incense and singing-bowl workshops, and the scent of Tibetan bread and butter tea. A guided morning here, timed to a monastery's puja with its horns and chanting, gives context the stupa alone cannot.

venues.name: Swayambhunath (the Monkey Temple)
venues.note: The valley's oldest and most iconic stupa, crowning a wooded hill reached by a steep flight of 365 stone steps guarded by troops of rhesus monkeys. The painted Buddha eyes gaze out over the whole of Kathmandu, and the fluttering prayer flags, the vajra and the mixed Hindu-Buddhist shrines make it a living crossroads of both faiths. For those who prefer not to climb, a private car reaches a side entrance near the top.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: Kathmandu Durbar Square & Hanuman Dhoka
venues.note: The medieval royal heart of the city, the old Hanuman Dhoka palace, a dense huddle of pagoda temples, the tall Kasthamandap and the coronation courtyards of the Malla and Shah kings. Some of it is still braced and rebuilding after 2015, which a good guide turns into a lesson in Newari craft rather than a caveat. Best walked slowly in early morning light before the square fills.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: The Kumari Ghar & the living goddess
venues.note: A superbly carved Newari courtyard house that is home to the Royal Kumari, a young girl worshipped as a living goddess, an incarnation of the goddess Taleju, who appears briefly at an upper window to those gathered below. It is one of the most singular living traditions on the subcontinent, and being present when she looks out is a quiet, unforgettable moment for a family. Photography of the goddess is forbidden.

venues.name: Patan Durbar Square & the Krishna Mandir
venues.note: The most refined of the valley's three royal squares, an open-air museum of Newari architecture where the stone Krishna Mandir, 21 gilded spires carved entirely from stone in 1637, stands among a forest of struts, courtyards and shrines. Just across the river from Kathmandu, it is calmer, greener and more intact than the capital's square, and instantly legible to Hindu visitors through its Krishna and Vishnu iconography.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: The Patan Museum
venues.note: Widely called one of the most beautiful museums in South Asia, set inside the restored Keshav Narayan Chowk palace and showing gilt-copper and cast-bronze Hindu and Buddhist deities at the very pinnacle of Newari metalwork. Around 300 masterpieces are displayed with rare restraint; the brick-and-timber galleries and the courtyard café make it a cultured, cool-of-the-day pause for all ages.

venues.name: The Patan metalwork & Newari craft workshops
venues.note: Patan is the valley's city of artisans, in the lanes around the Durbar Square, families still cast bronze and gilt-copper deities by the ancient lost-wax method, exactly as their ancestors did for the Malla kings. A private atelier visit lets a collector watch a statue take shape and commission a piece, a far more meaningful acquisition than anything on a shop shelf.

venues.name: Bhaktapur Durbar Square & the 55-Window Palace
venues.note: The best-preserved of the three royal cities, a car-free warren of ochre-brick lanes where the 55-Window Palace, the Golden Gate and the Lion Gate frame a square that feels frozen in the Malla age. Give it half a day with a guide; it rewards slow wandering more than any single monument in the valley, and children love its open, traffic-free stage.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: Bhaktapur Pottery Square
venues.note: An open square where potters still throw and sun-dry rows of clay pots and figurines in the traditional Prajapati way, as they have for centuries. Hands-on for children and quietly photogenic for everyone; a rare living-craft scene that has not been staged for visitors.

venues.name: Bhaktapur juju dhau, the King's Curd
venues.note: Bhaktapur's own delicacy: juju dhau, literally 'king of curds', a rich, faintly caramel yoghurt set in shallow clay bowls that give it its texture. Deeply vegetarian and utterly local, it is the perfect sweet pause between temples, and a taste that stays with you long after the trip.

venues.name: Changu Narayan Temple
venues.note: The oldest Hindu temple still in use in the valley, a double-roofed Vishnu shrine on a quiet wooded ridge, wrapped in some of the finest ancient stone and metal sculpture in Nepal, including a fifth-century Licchavi inscription, the country's oldest. Far less visited than the durbar squares, it pairs beautifully with Bhaktapur and speaks directly to Vaishnavite Hindu travellers.
credentials: UNESCO World Heritage Site, Kathmandu Valley

venues.name: Budhanilkantha, the Sleeping Vishnu
venues.note: Nepal's largest stone carving: a five-metre Vishnu reclining on the coils of the cosmic serpent Shesha, floating in a recessed pool that stands for the primordial ocean. For Hindus it is one of the valley's most powerful darshan, carved from a single block of black basalt in the Licchavi era; the early-morning ritual bathing of the deity is especially moving. A short drive north of the city, at the foot of the green Shivapuri hills.

venues.name: Kopan Monastery
venues.note: A serene Tibetan Buddhist monastery on a garden hill just above Boudhanath, famous worldwide for its meditation retreats and its calm, flower-filled courtyards looking out over the valley. Drop in for the free short guided meditation, watch the young monks debate, or arrange a private introduction to Buddhist practice, a restorative half-day that balances the intensity of the temples below.

venues.name: The Garden of Dreams
venues.note: A jewel-box neoclassical garden built in the 1920s by a Rana field marshal and lovingly restored with Austrian help, six pavilions for Nepal's six seasons, fountains, pergolas and lawns walled off from the roar of Thamel just outside. The most elegant place in central Kathmandu for a quiet coffee or a book; a genuine oasis for grandparents and children alike.

venues.name: Thamel, the buzz, and beyond it
venues.note: The pulsing tourist heart of Kathmandu: a lantern-lit maze of trekking-gear shops, pashmina and singing-bowl stores, rooftop cafés and live music. It is loud and energetic rather than luxurious, but an hour with a guide turns it into a rich hunt for the good, hand-knotted carpets, cashmere, thangkas and the best momos in town, while the rest is easily skipped.

venues.name: Asan & Indra Chowk bazaars
venues.note: The spice-and-textile soul of the old city, Asan is a six-way crossroads market trading everything from saffron and lentils to brass gods, while nearby Indra Chowk is the street of the bead sellers (pote), their stalls a river of coloured glass. Chaotic, fragrant and utterly authentic; walked with a guide it is the finest street-life theatre in the valley, and deeply familiar in rhythm to any Indian eye.

venues.name: Narayanhiti Palace Museum
venues.note: The former royal palace of the Shah kings, opened to the public after the monarchy fell in 2008, state rooms, thrones and, most hauntingly, the garden site of the 2001 royal massacre, marked and preserved. A sober, fascinating window into modern Nepal's history, a short walk from the smart shops of Durbar Marg. Photography is not permitted inside; closed Tuesdays and Wednesdays.

venues.name: Kirtipur old town
venues.area: Kirtipur hill, southwest of the city
venues.note: A time-warp Newari hill town of steep brick lanes, weavers at their looms and the twin temples of Bagh Bhairab and Uma Maheshwar, looking out over the whole valley to the Himalaya beyond. Barely touched by mass tourism, it offers the medieval texture of Bhaktapur without the crowds, a quiet favourite for travellers who have already seen the headline squares.

venues.name: Everest mountain flight
venues.note: A one-hour dawn flight along the length of the eastern Himalaya, every passenger guaranteed a window seat, that curls up to Everest itself and back, twenty peaks above the wing, the cockpit opened for a photograph of the summit. The single easiest way for grandparents and young children to stand eye-to-eye with the roof of the world. Best booked for clear-sky winter mornings (September to April); operated by Buddha Air and Yeti Airlines.

venues.name: Everest helicopter to Kala Patthar
venues.note: The ultimate valley-to-mountain day: a private helicopter northeast over Lukla and Tengboche to touch down on Kala Patthar (5,545m) beside Everest Base Camp, then breakfast on the terrace of the Hotel Everest View, the world's highest luxury hotel, with Everest, Lhotse, Nuptse and Ama Dablam filling the sky. Four to five hours door to door; altitude means it suits fit adults rather than the very young or elderly.

venues.name: Dhulikhel & the valley rim villages
venues.note: A handsome Newari town on the eastern rim with its own well-preserved temples and one of the best all-round Himalayan viewpoints near the capital, a favourite base for gentle rim walks. Quieter and more lived-in than Nagarkot, it makes a serene overnight for travellers wanting mountains, old streets and a slower pace in one place.

venues.name: Namobuddha Monastery
venues.note: One of the three holiest Buddhist sites in Nepal, on a hilltop where legend says a prince offered his body to a starving tigress, now crowned by the vast Thrangu Tashi Yangtse monastery and college, home to hundreds of monks. The drive out through terraced hills and a Newari village, and the 360-degree ridgetop view, make it a soulful day-trip, often walked as a gentle hike from Dhulikhel.

venues.name: Chandragiri Hills cable car
venues.note: A smooth ten-minute cable car glides up to a 2,551m ridge for a sweeping panorama of the valley and, on clear days, the Himalaya from Annapurna toward Everest, no trek required, ideal for multi-generational groups. At the top sit the Bhaleshwor Mahadev Shiva temple, cafés and a resort; a soft-adventure half-day that even the least mobile grandparent can share.

venues.name: Krishnarpan at Dwarika's, the Newari feast
venues.note: The valley's definitive fine-dining experience: a ceremonial Newari banquet of six to as many as twenty-two courses, served on painted earthenware and brass, opening with the traditional Samaya Baji platter. Set inside Dwarika's, a heritage hotel that is itself a living museum of rescued Newari woodcarving and a UNESCO conservation-award winner, it is deeply vegetarian-friendly and the single most refined table in Kathmandu.

venues.name: Momos & the Newari table
venues.note: No visit is complete without momos, the steamed dumpling that is Kathmandu's true street food, alongside a proper Newari spread of bara, chatamari (the 'Newari pizza'), yomari and the tang of aloo achar. Almost every dish has a rich vegetarian version, and a guided food walk through the old city, or a private Newari cooking session, is a warm, hands-on window into the valley for the whole family.

venues.name: Singing bowls & sound healing
venues.note: The valley is the world's home of the Himalayan singing bowl, and the best ateliers around Thamel and Boudha will teach you to read a bowl by its tone or lead a private sound-healing session, resonance you feel in the chest rather than merely hear. A restorative, characterful souvenir and experience in one, and a gentle counterpoint to days of temples.

venues.name: Thangka painting ateliers
venues.note: In the studios around Boudhanath and Patan, master painters still create thangkas, sacred scroll paintings of deities and mandalas, with single-hair brushes and mineral pigments, some pieces taking months of meditative work. A private studio visit lets a collector understand the iconography and commission a genuinely museum-grade piece, not a tourist print.

venues.name: Boudhanath butter-lamp dusk & rooftop dinner
venues.note: As evening falls the stupa is ringed with hundreds of flickering butter lamps and the low hum of prayer, and the smart move is a candlelit table on one of the circle's rooftop restaurants looking straight down onto the dome. Among the most atmospheric, and calmest, dinners in the valley, and a fitting close to a day of monasteries.

venues.name: Private heritage walk of the old city
venues.note: The medieval fabric of Kathmandu lives in the lanes and hidden courtyards (bahals and bahis) between the durbar square and Asan, carved windows, forgotten shrines, artisan alleys that no map quite captures. Walked at dawn with a specialist Newari-culture guide, before the traffic wakes, it is the richest and most personal way to read the city's thousand years.

venues.name: Shivapuri Nagarjun National Park walk
venues.note: A green forested reserve on the valley's northern edge, laced with walking trails to the Shivapuri peak, hidden gompas and viewpoints over the whole basin, birdsong, waterfalls and cool air minutes from the city's dust. A gentle guided nature morning that suits families wanting movement and quiet between the temple days.

venues.name: Seto Machhendranath & the old-city processions
venues.note: Tucked in a courtyard off the Asan-Indra Chowk axis, this white Avalokiteshvara/Machhendranath temple is one of the most revered in the old city and the focus of a great annual chariot procession beloved of both Hindus and Buddhists. Timed with a guide to a puja or festival, it shows the living, shared devotion that still animates Kathmandu's lanes.

venues.name: Boudha & Patan by dawn light for photography
venues.note: The valley's monuments are transformed in the first hour of light, the Boudha kora nearly empty, Patan's struts and spires gilded, monks sweeping the courtyards. A private photography-led morning with an expert, before the tour groups arrive, yields both the images and the stillness that the middle of the day cannot.

venues.name: Pashupatinath Bagmati Aarti at dusk
venues.note: Each evening on the Bagmati's terraces, robed priests perform the aarti, a choreography of fire, lamps, bells and conch, echoing the great river rituals of Varanasi and Haridwar. Watched from the far bank as the ghats glow and the chants rise, it is among the most spiritually charged half-hours in the Himalaya, and speaks straight to the Hindu heart.

venues.name: Barc
venues.note: An intimate speakeasy hidden inside an office block, Nepali ingredients, world-class technique, and the finest bar in the country.
credentials: Asia's 50 Best Bars 2025, No. 35 (the first Nepalese bar ever to make the list)
Michter's Art of Hospitality Award 2025, Asia's 50 Best Bars

venues.name: Bitters & Co.
venues.note: An airy, high-ceilinged room bringing international cocktail culture to the city, an Old Fashioned served in a smoke-filled box, a clarified milk punch worth the visit.
credentials: World's 50 Best Bars, 50 Best Discovery (Kathmandu)
Asia's 50 Best Bars 2023, No. 69

venues.name: The Dwarika's bar
venues.note: A quiet drink within the carved Newari courtyards of Nepal's most decorated house, the calmest, most considered evening in the city.
credentials: Genuine standing, the bar at The Dwarika's Hotel, holder of Nepal's first MICHELIN Key (2025)
